concepts.title: Representing Scenes with Fields
concepts.one_liner: Fields are general-purpose functions that vary over space, mapping coordinates to values to represent scenes.
concepts.content: Fields are a way to represent functions that vary over space and are used as a scene representation in many contexts. For example, every image is a field: it is a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values. While images in computer vision are often discrete fields where input coordinates are discrete-valued, fields can also be continuous. Furthermore, fields can be more than two-dimensional and can even be defined over non-Euclidean geometries like the surface of a sphere. Radiance fields are a specific example of vector fields, which assign a vector to each position in space, such as a mapping $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$ where $X, Y, Z$ are coordinates and $v_1, v_2$ are values.
concepts.motivation_md: Fields provide a unified mathematical framework for representing diverse spatial data, from 2D images to 3D volumes and complex physical properties like light radiance.
concepts.recap_md: - Fields map spatial coordinates to specific values or vectors.

concepts.title: Vector Fields
concepts.one_liner: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.
concepts.content: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, we might have a vector field $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are some values. Radiance fields are a specific example of this type of function.
concepts.motivation_md: Vector fields allow us to describe properties that have both magnitude and direction (or multiple components) at every point in a spatial domain.
concepts.recap_md: - A vector field maps spatial coordinates to a vector of values.

Radiance fields are a specific example of this type of function.

concepts.title: Pixel Images as Fields
concepts.one_liner: Pixel images are discrete fields mapping 2D coordinates to color values.
concepts.content: Pixel images, $f: x, y \rightarrow r, g, b$, are fields with the property that the input domain is discrete, or, equivalently, the field is piecewise constant over little squares that tile the space.
concepts.motivation_md: Treating an image as a field allows us to apply signal processing and functional analysis tools to digital pictures.
concepts.recap_md: - Pixel images are discrete fields mapping $(x, y)$ to $(r, g, b)$ values.

slots.motivation: Treating an image as a field allows us to apply signal processing and functional analysis tools to digital pictures.
slots.key_passage: - Pixel images are discrete fields mapping $(x, y)$ to $(r, g, b)$ values.
slots.example: Pixel images, $f: x, y \rightarrow r, g, b$, are fields with the property that the input domain is discrete, or, equivalently, the field is piecewise constant over little squares that tile the space.

concepts.title: Voxel Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel fields are discrete 3D fields representing values like occupancy or color in a volume.
concepts.content: Voxel fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$ are discrete fields that can represent values $\mathbf{v}$ like spatial occupancy, flux, or color in a volume. They are like 3D pixels. Like pixels, they have the special property that they are piecewise constant over cubes the size of their resolution.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxels extend the concept of 2D pixels into 3D space to represent volumetric data.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxel fields are the 3D equivalent of pixel images.

slots.motivation: Voxels extend the concept of 2D pixels into 3D space to represent volumetric data.
slots.key_passage: - Voxel fields are the 3D equivalent of pixel images.

Like pixels, they have the special property that they are piecewise constant over cubes the size of their resolution.

concepts.title: Optical Flow Fields
concepts.one_liner: Optical flow fields measure motion by mapping image coordinates and time to velocity vectors.
concepts.content: Optical flow fields, $f: x, y, t \rightarrow u, v$, measure motion in a video in terms of how scene content flows across the image plane.
concepts.motivation_md: Optical flow is essential for tracking objects and understanding temporal dynamics in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Optical flow maps $(x, y, t)$ to motion vectors $(u, v)$.

slots.motivation: Optical flow is essential for tracking objects and understanding temporal dynamics in video sequences.
slots.key_passage: - Optical flow maps $(x, y, t)$ to motion vectors $(u, v)$.

concepts.title: Signed Distance Functions (SDFs)
concepts.one_liner: Signed distance functions represent geometry by mapping points to their distance from the closest surface.
concepts.content: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation of geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: SDFs provide a mathematically clean way to define surfaces and perform geometric operations like boolean unions or intersections.
concepts.recap_md: - SDFs map 3D coordinates to the distance to the nearest surface.

slots.motivation: SDFs provide a mathematically clean way to define surfaces and perform geometric operations like boolean unions or intersections.
slots.key_passage: - SDFs map 3D coordinates to the distance to the nearest surface.

concepts.title: Implicit vs. Explicit Representations

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Implicit representations use parameterized functions to represent continuous fields with infinite resolution.
concepts.content: Continuous fields are powerful because they have infinite resolution. However, we cannot represent a continuous field explicitly by recording the value at all infinite possible positions. Instead, we use an implicit representation: we record a finite set of parameters for a function that can tell us the value of the field at any coordinate. These parameterized functions take as input any continuous position and return the field value at that location.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit representations allow us to store and manipulate continuous, high-resolution data using a manageable, finite number of parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit representations store function parameters rather than raw values.

slots.motivation: Implicit representations allow us to store and manipulate continuous, high-resolution data using a manageable, finite number of parameters.

These parameterized functions take as input any continuous position and return the field value at that location.

concepts.title: Differentiable Radiance Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Differentiable radiance fields use gradient-based optimization to fit parameterized functions to scene images.
concepts.content: There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that could represent a target radiance field $L$, such as neural networks or mixtures of Gaussians. The important property is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is a differentiable function of the parameters $\theta$. This allows the use of gradient-based optimization to find parameter settings that yield a desirable field. Whatever function family is used, it takes coordinates as input and produces colors and densities as output (see figure: Module for a parameterized radiance field. We use $\mathbf{R}$ to denote the vector of coordinates $L_\theta$ takes as input.). Because these functions are differentiable, they can be treated as modules in a computation graph, allowing for the use of backpropagation to fit the field to a set of images.
concepts.motivation_md: By making the radiance field differentiable, we can use standard machine learning optimization techniques to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Radiance fields are represented by differentiable functions $L_{\theta}$.

slots.motivation: By making the radiance field differentiable, we can use standard machine learning optimization techniques to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images.
slots.key_passage: - Radiance fields are represented by differentiable functions $L_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: Radiance Field
concepts.one_liner: A radiance field models a scene's optical content as a function mapping coordinates and viewing angles to color and density values.
concepts.motivation_md: Radiance fields allow for the representation of complex scenes with view-dependent effects like specular highlights, which traditional mesh-based or point-based reconstructions struggle to capture accurately.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to color ($r,g,b$) and density ($\sigma$).

slots.motivation: Radiance fields allow for the representation of complex scenes with view-dependent effects like specular highlights, which traditional mesh-based or point-based reconstructions struggle to capture accurately.
slots.key_passage: - Maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to color ($r,g,b$) and density ($\sigma$).

concepts.title: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model a radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$, typically a multilayer perceptron.
concepts.content: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) are a popular way of parameterizing a radiance field $L_{\theta}$. NeRFs model the radiance field $L$ with a neural network $L_{\theta}$. The neural network architecture in the original NeRF is a multilayer perceptron (MLP), but other architectures could be used as well. For the MLP formulation, evaluating the color-density at a single coordinate corresponds to a single forward pass through an MLP.
concepts.motivation_md: NeRFs provide a continuous, differentiable representation of a 3D scene's radiance and density, allowing for high-quality view synthesis using standard neural network architectures.
concepts.recap_md: - NeRFs parameterize the radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$.

slots.motivation: NeRFs provide a continuous, differentiable representation of a 3D scene's radiance and density, allowing for high-quality view synthesis using standard neural network architectures.
slots.key_passage: - NeRFs parameterize the radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$.

concepts.title: NeRF as 1x1 Convolutional Neural Network

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: When querying a grid of coordinates, a NeRF behaves like a convolutional neural network with 1x1 filters.
concepts.content:
Often we want to evaluate the color-density at multiple coordinate locations. To create an explicit representation of the field's values at a grid of coordinates, we can query the field on this grid. In this usage, the NeRF $L_{\theta}$ looks like a convolutional neural network (CNN) with 1x1 filters, as this is the architecture that results from applying an MLP to each position in a grid of inputs. concepts.title: Fourier Positional Encodings

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Fourier positional encodings transform raw coordinates into a representation that helps neural networks model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. In fact, the same positional encoding scheme is used as in transformers. @fig-nerfs-flatland_positional_encoding shows how this scheme translates the $XY$-coordinate field of Flatland to positional encodings:

(see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network to model high frequencies variations, which are abundant in radiance fields. In regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than it is to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias will be reduced. This makes it so the MLP has an easier time fitting high frequency functions that change in value rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to the locations $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency details in 3D scenes (the 'spectral bias'). Positional encodings map inputs to a higher-dimensional space where these variations are easier to learn.
concepts.recap_md: - Fourier positional encodings reduce the bias of MLPs toward low-frequency functions.

concepts.title: Voxel-based Radiance Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel-based radiance fields parameterize 3D scenes using a grid-based volumetric representation.
concepts.content: One alternative to neural parameterization is to parameterize the radiance fields using a voxel-based representation.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxel-based representations can offer faster training and rendering times compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs by storing scene data in an explicit grid.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxel-based fields use a discrete grid (voxels) to store radiance and density values.

slots.motivation: Voxel-based representations can offer faster training and rendering times compared to pure MLP-based NeRFs by storing scene data in an explicit grid.
slots.key_passage: - Voxel-based fields use a discrete grid (voxels) to store radiance and density values.

concepts.title: Gaussian Mixture Radiance Fields
concepts.one_liner: Gaussian mixture radiance fields approximate scene content using a collection of semi-transparent ellipsoids with specific colors and densities.
concepts.content: Another alternative is to use a mixture of Gaussians. In this case, each Gaussian represents a semi-transparent ellipsoid of some color $\mathbf{c}$ and some density $\sigma$. When many such Gaussians overlap, their sum can approximate scene content very well.
concepts.motivation_md: Using Gaussians allows for a more flexible, non-grid-aligned representation of geometry that can be more efficient than voxels for certain types of scene content.
concepts.recap_md: - Scenes are modeled as a sum of overlapping semi-transparent ellipsoids.

slots.motivation: Using Gaussians allows for a more flexible, non-grid-aligned representation of geometry that can be more efficient than voxels for certain types of scene content.

concepts.title: View Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: View synthesis is the process of rendering a scene from novel camera viewpoints using its underlying radiance field representation.
concepts.content: Radiance fields can be useful for many tasks in scene modeling, as they represent both appearance and geometry (density) of content in 3D. However, the main purpose they were introduced for is view synthesis. This is the problem of rendering what a scene looks like from different camera viewpoints. In the Flatland example, this is the problem of rendering the set of 1D images, $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, shown on the left of @fig-nerfs-flatland_cameras_and_images. Once you have a radiance field for a scene, you can solve view synthesis by rendering images from it.
concepts.motivation_md: View synthesis allows for the creation of photorealistic images from angles where no original photos were taken, which is essential for VR, AR, and special effects.
concepts.recap_md: - View synthesis renders new camera viewpoints from a 3D scene representation.

slots.motivation: View synthesis allows for the creation of photorealistic images from angles where no original photos were taken, which is essential for VR, AR, and special effects.
slots.key_passage: - View synthesis renders new camera viewpoints from a 3D scene representation.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering is a strategy for rendering images by integrating radiance values along camera rays through a volume of density.
concepts.content: Volume rendering is the strategy that methods like NeRFs use for rendering images from radiance fields. Volume rendering works by taking an integral of the radiance values along each camera ray. Think of it like looking into a hazy volume of colored dust. The integral adds up all the color values along the camera ray, weighted by a value related to the density of the dust. A cartoon visualization of the process is given in @fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering, and several real results of rendering radiance fields are shown in @fig-nerfs-flatland_training.
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering provides a differentiable way to map a 3D volume (density and color) to a 2D image, which is necessary for training neural networks on image data.
concepts.recap_md: - Volume rendering integrates color along a ray, weighted by local density.

slots.motivation: Volume rendering provides a differentiable way to map a 3D volume (density and color) to a 2D image, which is necessary for training neural networks on image data.
slots.key_passage: - Volume rendering integrates color along a ray, weighted by local density.

A cartoon visualization of the process is given in @fig-nerfs-flatland_volume_rendering, and several real results of rendering radiance fields are shown in @fig-nerfs-flatland_training.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Equation
concepts.one_liner: The volume rendering equation maps a radiance field to an image by integrating color and density along rays passing through pixels.
concepts.content:
The volume rendering equation is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
where $r(t)$ gives the coordinates, in the radiance field, of a point $t$ distance along the ray, $\mathbf{D}$ is the direction of the ray (a unit vector), and $t_n$ and $t_f$ are the near and far cutoff points, respectively. We only integrate over the region of the ray within an interval sufficiently large to capture the scene content of interest. To render an image, we can apply this equation to the ray that passes through each pixel in the image. This procedure maps a radiance field $L$ to an image $\boldsymbol\ell$ as viewed by some camera.
concepts.motivation_md: This equation mathematically formalizes how light travels through and is absorbed by a semi-transparent medium, allowing for the calculation of final pixel colors from a 3D field.
concepts.recap_md:
- The equation integrates color $L^c$ and density $L^\sigma$ along a ray $r(t)$.
- The term $\alpha(t)$ represents the transmittance (how much light reaches the camera).

slots.key_passage:

- The term $\alpha(t)$ represents the transmittance (how much light reaches the camera).

concepts.title: Colored Particle Model
concepts.one_liner: A model that treats volume as being filled with colored particles, where observed color depends on the probability of a ray hitting particles along its path.
concepts.content: This model is based on the idea that space is filled with colored particles. When a ray is traced from the camera into the scene, it may hit one of these particles, determining the observed color. For any given increment along the ray, there is a chance of not hitting a particle. This is modeled by the density function $L^\sigma$, representing the differential probability of hitting a particle. The probability of not hitting a particle up to distance $t$ is given by $\alpha$, a cumulative integral of densities. The integral in @eq-nerfs-vol_rendering_integral averages over the colors of all the particles we might hit along the ray, weighted by the probability of hitting them.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a physical intuition for volume rendering by treating space as a probabilistic medium of particles rather than just abstract mathematical integrals.
concepts.recap_md: - Space is modeled as being filled with colored particles with a specific density $L^\sigma$.

slots.motivation: It provides a physical intuition for volume rendering by treating space as a probabilistic medium of particles rather than just abstract mathematical integrals.
slots.key_passage: - Space is modeled as being filled with colored particles with a specific density $L^\sigma$.

concepts.title: Ray Casting
concepts.one_liner: A special case of volume rendering where the ray terminates at the first solid surface it hits.
concepts.content: Ray casting is a special case of volume rendering that occurs when particle density is either zero (empty space) or infinite (solid objects). In empty space, the density is zero and contributes nothing to the integral. When a ray hits a solid object with infinite density, the transparency $\alpha$ immediately goes to zero, and the ray terminates at the surface. Consequently, if a scene consists only of solid objects and empty space, volume rendering reduces to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera. This simple model is how many basic renderers work, including standard rasterization pipelines @shirley2009fundamentals.
concepts.motivation_md: It simplifies complex volume rendering into a more intuitive model for scenes containing only solid objects, serving as the basis for many standard renderers.
concepts.recap_md: - Ray casting occurs when volume rendering is applied to scenes with only solid objects and empty space.

slots.motivation: It simplifies complex volume rendering into a more intuitive model for scenes containing only solid objects, serving as the basis for many standard renderers.
slots.key_passage: - Ray casting occurs when volume rendering is applied to scenes with only solid objects and empty space.
slots.example: Ray casting is a special case of volume rendering that occurs when particle density is either zero (empty space) or infinite (solid objects). In empty space, the density is zero and contributes nothing to the integral. concepts.title: Quadrature Rule for Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: A discrete approximation of the volume rendering integral using a sum of samples along a ray.
concepts.content: To compute the volume rendering integral, it can be approximated as a discrete sum using a quadrature rule (see @max1995optical, @max2005local). The approximation is given by: $$\begin{aligned} \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\ \alpha_i &= \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\ \delta_i &= t_{i+1} - t_i \end{aligned}$$ Here, the continuous radiance field is replaced by a discrete vector of samples $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$, where $\mathbf{R}_t = r(t)$ is the world coordinate at distance $t$ along ray $r$. (see figure: Volume rendering of our Flatland radiance field.) In this procedure, rays are sampled at specific points (circles). The size of each circle indicates the $\alpha$ value, while the color and transparency indicate the radiance field's density and color at that point. For solid objects, density is infinite, causing $\alpha$ to go to zero for all subsequent points along the ray.
concepts.motivation_md: Continuous integrals cannot be computed directly by computers, so a discrete quadrature rule is necessary to numerically estimate the light accumulated along a ray.
concepts.recap_md: - The continuous volume rendering integral is approximated using a discrete sum of samples along the ray.

concepts.title: Stochastic Sampling Along Rays
concepts.one_liner: A sampling strategy that divides a ray into intervals and samples one point uniformly from each to ensure continuous coverage.
concepts.content: Instead of taking samples at evenly spaced increments, as suggested in @mildenhall2020nerf, the ray is divided into $T$ evenly spaced intervals, and one point is sampled uniformly within each interval. This ensures that all continuous coordinates have a probability of being sampled. Over multiple iterations of an optimization loop, every point in the continuous space will eventually be supervised. For a ray with origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$, the sampled coordinates $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ are computed as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R}_i &= \mathbf{O} + t_i\mathbf{D}\\ t_i &\sim \mathcal{U}[i-1,i]*\frac{t_f-t_n}{T}+t_n \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathcal{U}[a,b]$ is the uniform distribution over the interval $[a,b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Fixed-step sampling can miss details between samples; stochastic sampling ensures that the entire volume is eventually seen and supervised during the training process.
concepts.recap_md: - The ray is partitioned into $T$ equal segments, with one point sampled randomly from each.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Computation Graph
concepts.one_liner: A modular pipeline that maps pixel coordinates to color values through ray generation, sampling, and volume integration.
concepts.content: The full volume rendering pipeline is defined as a series of computational modules. To find the color of a pixel $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$ at camera coordinates $n,m$, the first step is to determine the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) passing through it. This uses the camera origin $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$ and the camera matrix $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$, which maps pixel coordinates to world coordinates (see @sec-pixel_to_rays). (see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.) RGB images are represented as $N \times M \times 3$ dimensional arrays. Next, world coordinates are sampled along the ray (see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.) Finally, the volume rendering integral is computed using a quadrature rule to determine the pixel's color (see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.) This pipeline maps pixel coordinates to $r,g,b$ color values.
concepts.motivation_md: Organizing the rendering process into a modular computation graph allows for the use of automatic differentiation and backpropagation to optimize scene representations.
concepts.recap_md: - The pipeline maps pixel coordinates to rays, samples points along those rays, and integrates their colors.

concepts.title: Fitting Radiance Fields as an Inverse Problem

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: The process of inferring a 3D radiance field from 2D images by treating rendering as an inverse problem.
concepts.content: The goal is to find a radiance field $L_{\theta}$ that explains a set of observed images. While rendering a radiance field into images (view synthesis) is a graphics problem, inferring the field from images is a vision problem, specifically an inverse problem. This is the task denizens of Flatland solve as they walk around their world to represent the scene they see. The fitting procedure takes a set of images $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}, \mathbf{K}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}, \mathbf{O}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}\}_{i=1}^N$ as input to produce a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$. The objective is to ensure that when the resulting radiance field is rendered using the input camera parameters, the output matches the original images as closely as possible.
concepts.motivation_md: To reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D photos, we must treat the rendering process as a function to be inverted, allowing us to solve for the underlying scene parameters.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is treated as the inverse problem of graphics: inferring the scene from its rendered images.

concepts.title: Full NeRF Rendering Pipeline

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: A differentiable computation graph that uses volume rendering to generate images from a parameterized radiance field.
concepts.content: Given a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$, an image is rendered using the volume rendering process described previously. The entire computation graph is differentiable, which is critical for fitting parameters to data. (see figure: Full NeRF pipeline for rendering an image.) Camera parameters are input into the $\texttt{pixel2ray}$ module, and $\texttt{vrender}$ takes the direction $\mathbf{D}$ and sampling points $\mathbf{t}$ computed by $\texttt{ray2coords}$ to produce the final output.
concepts.motivation_md: A fully differentiable pipeline allows for the use of gradient-based optimization to learn the parameters of a radiance field from image data.
concepts.recap_md: - The pipeline is composed of differentiable modules, enabling end-to-end optimization via backpropagation.

prereq.rationale: To fit a radiance field, one must first understand what a radiance field is as the target representation.
The pipeline uses the volume rendering process to generate the images that are compared against ground truth data.
The pipeline is the technical implementation of the inverse problem fitting strategy described in the previous concept.
The pipeline specifically operates on a parameterized radiance field, which is the core of the NeRF definition.
Implicit representations are introduced as a method to represent continuous fields like radiance fields without discrete sampling.
Differentiable radiance fields are a specific application of implicit representations using parameterized functions.
NeRF is a specific and popular method for parameterizing differentiable radiance fields.
This concept describes the specific behavior and architectural interpretation of a NeRF when queried on a grid.
Fourier positional encoding is a critical technique used in NeRFs to enable the modeling of high-frequency scene details.
Voxel-based radiance fields are a specific implementation of the general radiance field concept using a grid-based representation.
This concept applies the general voxel field data structure to the specific task of parameterizing radiance and density.
Gaussian mixture radiance fields are a specific way to parameterize the radiance and density functions of a scene.
View synthesis is the primary problem that radiance fields were designed to solve by enabling rendering from novel viewpoints.
The quadrature rule is the discrete numerical approximation used to compute the continuous volume rendering integral.
Stochastic sampling is a specific technique for choosing the sample points used in the quadrature approximation.
The pipeline includes a module specifically for sampling coordinates along the generated rays.
Vector fields are a specific type of the general field representation used in scene modeling.

overlay.rationale: The text explicitly contrasts the graphics problem (view synthesis) with the vision problem (the inverse problem of fitting).
The full pipeline provides a concrete implementation of a differentiable radiance field system.
Voxel-based representations are presented as an alternative to the neural parameterization used in NeRFs.
Volume rendering is the specific strategy used to perform view synthesis from a radiance field representation.
The volume rendering equation provides the rigorous mathematical definition of the volume rendering strategy.
The colored particle model provides the physical intuition for the terms (density, color, transparency) in the volume rendering integral.
Ray casting is a special case of volume rendering where density is binary, causing rays to terminate at the first solid surface.
The general concept of fields as scene representations is illustrated by the specific case of radiance fields introduced earlier.
Vector fields are the broader class of functions to which radiance fields belong.
Pixel images are presented as a discrete, 2D special case of the more general field representation.
Voxel fields are presented as a discrete, 3D special case of the more general field representation.
Voxel fields extend the 2D discrete field concept of pixels into three dimensions.
Optical flow is a specific type of vector field where the vectors represent motion velocity.
SDFs are a specific type of field that maps spatial coordinates to scalar distance values.
